section_summary: This section opens with an American Embassy despatch reporting the suppression of the February 1, 1940 issue of Gaiko Jiho and reproduces Tsuneo Yonaiyama’s lengthy critique of Japan’s conduct and objectives in the war in China. It then documents New Year messages published by Japanese Abroad, including diplomatic greetings and George de Ghika’s survey of Japanese-Hungarian cultural relations, followed by two cross-reference slips. The final portion contains correspondence with the Japan Institute and much of its brochure Samples of Replies to Inquiries on Things Japanese, illustrating its dissemination of information about Japanese society, culture, government, war mobilization, and postal services.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4595: Suppression of Gaiko Jiho of February 1, 1940
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Home Office’s suppression of a Gaiko Jiho issue containing Tsuneo Yonaiyama’s article on the war in China.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese Home Office suppressed the February 1 issue of Gaiko Jiho and confiscated copies because of Yonaiyama’s “Keynote for the Settlement of the China Incident”; the author was subsequently forced to resign from the Foreign Office. The Embassy summarizes his argument that Japan is fighting a prolonged war rather than a limited incident, that Chinese resistance cannot be overcome through Wang Ching-wei or abstract pan-Asian ideals, and that continental expansion could threaten Japan itself. Grew interprets the article as evidence of policy conflict within the Japanese government and a growing recognition that hegemony over China may be unattainable.

subfiles.title: Keynote for the Settlement of the China Incident
subfiles.doc_type: translated periodical article; enclosure to Despatch No. 4595
subfiles.from: Tsuneo Yonaiyama; translated by the American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.to: Readers of Gaiko Jiho and the Department of State
subfiles.about: Argues that the China conflict is a protracted war whose settlement must be based on practical Japanese interests rather than pan-Asian ideals.
subfiles.summary: Yonaiyama contrasts the official designation of the fighting as an “incident” with Nobuyuki Abe’s admission that it is an unprecedented war, and contends that such a war would ordinarily require a commensurate prize. Drawing on the 1932 Shanghai fighting, Chinese military logistics, and Qing and Mongol history, he warns that conquering and holding China’s interior would exhaust Japan. He characterizes both Chiang Kai-shek’s armed resistance and Wang Ching-wei’s accommodation as forms of Chinese national resistance. The article rejects an East Asia bloc and asks whether Japan should antagonize Europe and the United States when its real enemy is closer at hand.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs abstract of Despatch No. 5299
subfiles.doc_type: Department of State office memorandum and abstract
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Embassy’s report on diplomatic New Year messages and an anti-American editorial in Japanese Abroad.
subfiles.summary: Abstract of Despatch 5299: the magazine printed greetings from the American and British ambassadors and the Hungarian minister's essay on cultural exchange, but the same issue had a long attack, "The United States is Dancing on a Volcano."

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5299: January issue of Japanese Abroad
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards diplomatic greetings and an article printed in Japanese Abroad and comments on the magazine’s attack on American policy.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards his New Year greeting, the British ambassador's and the Hungarian minister's article on cultural relations, and the editor's "The United States is Dancing on a Volcano," blaming American policy on jealousy, a superiority complex and desire for world conquest, which he finds unworthy of summary.

subfiles.title: Letter to Nakamura concerning a New Year message
subfiles.about: Provides a restrained New Year greeting for Japanese Abroad while warning that international relations depend on actions rather than assurances.
subfiles.summary: Grew declines broad claims about international understanding now, saying messages count for little against actions, but lets Nakamura publish the enclosed brief goodwill message.

subfiles.title: New Year message to Japanese Abroad
subfiles.about: Offers good wishes for the magazine’s contribution to international friendship and understanding.
subfiles.summary: Grew sends Japanese Abroad New Year wishes and hopes it keeps promoting understanding between nations.

subfiles.title: British ambassador’s New Year greeting
subfiles.from: R. L. Craigie, British Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Offers New Year greetings to the Oriental Culture Society and Japanese Abroad.
subfiles.summary: Craigie agrees international understanding is paramount, hopes the Oriental Culture Society keeps countering deliberately inspired misconceptions, and wishes it success.

subfiles.title: Development of Japanese-Hungarian Cultural Relations
subfiles.doc_type: periodical article; enclosure to Despatch No. 5299
subfiles.from: George de Ghika, Minister of Hungary
subfiles.about: Surveys the individuals, societies, and agreements that fostered cultural exchange between Japan and Hungary.
subfiles.summary: De Ghika traces Japanese-Hungarian cultural ties from the First World War through societies, language study, scholarly visits, translations and arts, stressing the 1938 Cultural Pact and mixed committees, and says Hungary's Tripartite Pact adherence should deepen cooperation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Foreign Minister’s address before the America-Japan Society
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to Despatch No. 5259 concerning reports of a Japan News Week editorial about the foreign minister’s address.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's Despatch 5259 on a December 21, 1940 Japan News Week editorial, file 711.94/1940.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 756 concerning Japan News Week
subfiles.about: Refers to a Grew despatch concerning Japan News Week and its connection with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 756 (July 30, 1941), file 811.7181/365, on Japan News Week, the U.S. and an enclosed editorial.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Nippon and Japan Institute publications
subfiles.from: Charles A. Thomson, Division of Cultural Relations, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Nippon and the Japan Institute pamphlet Replies to Inquiries on Things Japanese.
subfiles.summary: Thomson thanks Mayeda for the illustrated quarterly Nippon and the pamphlet on the Japan Institute's information service, and for its service to those interested in Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Nippon and Replies to Inquiries on Things Japanese
subfiles.to: Charles A. Thomson, Division of Cultural Relations, Department of State
subfiles.about: Sends the Department of State an issue of Nippon and a pamphlet demonstrating the Japan Institute’s reference service.
subfiles.summary: Mayeda sends Nippon No. 22 with subscription information for its American agent, encloses "Replies to Inquiries on Things Japanese" as an example of the Institute's service, and offers further answers.

subfiles.title: Samples of Replies to Inquiries on Things Japanese
subfiles.to: General readers and prospective users of the Institute’s information service
subfiles.about: Presents examples of the Japan Institute’s answers to American and Canadian inquiries about Japanese culture, industry, history, government, and daily life.
subfiles.summary: The brochure explains the Institute’s reference service and reproduces sample answers on rayon production, herbalism and astrology, Obon, Takayama Hikokurō, North Pacific fisheries, bonsai, gourds, forests, constitutional war powers, military service, cherry trees, Japanese music, Noh, and vocational education. Later examples describe the Planning Board, women’s wartime activities, and postal rates. The responses mix statistics, historical narratives, bibliographical references, and explanations of government institutions and popular customs. The surviving section ends in the middle of the answer on articles prohibited from the Japanese mails.
